text.p: Maanshan Iron and Steel Co Ltd's profits this year will surpass the 1995 level but investors should not get over-optimistic about the company's near-term prospects, Su Jiangang, secretary to the board, said on Monday.
China's two interest rate cuts this year would help ease strains on the big steelmaker but they would not offset a number of factors that have pressured results, he said.
"We will have better results this year but don't get overoptimistic," he told reporters at an investment seminar.

Maanshan, which has so-called H shares listed in Hong Kong and A shares for Chinese investors trading in Shanghai, posted net profits of 43 million yuan ($5.18 million) last year, down from 749 million yuan in 1994 and 1.35 billion yuan in 1993.
Su said that even over the next few years the company was unlikely to return to the 1993 levels when rapid growth in the domestic market pushed steel prices sharply higher.
Maanshan has been badly affected by China's tight credit policies which have made many of the company's big customers unable to pay off their debts.
Bad and non-performing debts this year would not be below last year's level of 240 million yuan, the official said.
Receivables would be between 900 million and 1.0 billion yuan, though that would be down from the 1.2 billion at the end of last year, he said.
Finished steel inventories were now about 40,000 tonnes, down from 60,000 a year ago.
Su also said that rising costs would continue to affect the company as it is unable to sharply increase the price of its products.

Maanshan is a major consumer of coal and state controls on the fuel are gradually being eased. Domestic coal prices are now about 40 to 50 yuan per tonne below world prices, the official said, adding that the gap will narrow in future.

The company's output of steel products would rise to 2.15 million tonnes this year from 1.92 million last year and pig iron production would climb to 3.63 million tonnes from 3.24 million, the official said.
